records.name: Philadelphia Film Factory
records.summary: A film education group for local independent filmmakers. It runs beginner classes on making films, writing scripts and acting on camera, plus Take One, a youth film program that offers paid internships.
records.what_you_do: Take a beginner class such as Intro to Filmmaking or Intro to Screenwriting, come to a networking event, or ask about Take One, the youth program with paid internships.

schedule.text: Beginner classes run about six weeks and usually meet on weeknight evenings, for example Monday and Wednesday from 6 to 9 pm. Each round's dates are posted on its class page.

locations.label: Studio days (students arrange their own travel)

cost.text: Beginner classes are paid courses, and each round sets its own price. The 2026 Intro to Filmmaking page listed $1,250, or $1,000 for paying in full early, and the Intro to Screenwriting page listed $500. Take One offers paid internships.

requirements.gear: Binder or folders, pens and a notepad. A laptop or tablet is highly recommended for the intro course.

first_step.how: Email info@philmfactory.org to ask when the next beginner class opens. The spring 2026 applications were due by March 24, 2026.
first_step.basis: Beginner classes are written for total beginners, and each class page has an application form to fill in before you start.
first_step.what_to_expect: Each beginner course runs about six weeks in weeknight sessions, and students make a short film or script as a group. Payment is due up front or on an installment plan, and the intro film course starts with a mandatory orientation. Studio days happen in Clifton Heights, so plan your own ride, and the adult courses are for people 18 and older.
first_visit_tips: Bring a laptop or tablet if you have one, since the intro course calls it highly recommended.
Bring a notebook, folders and pens.
Plan your own ride to the studio days in Clifton Heights, PA.
Plan to attend the mandatory orientation at the Cambridge Innovation Center, 3675 Market St, 8th floor.

records.notes: The group's own site calls it Philm Factory; the name field keeps the name from our earlier data. Correction to tier 1: Take One is described as paid internships, and the page does not call it free. The spring 2026 class deadlines have passed. Closed classes (Cinematography 101, On-Camera Acting, Assistant Directing, Advance Acting) point to a wait list form, which was not submitted. No accessibility information on the site. Take One age range, schedule and application deadline are not stated.

records.name: Philadelphia Justice Project for Women & Girls
records.summary: A Philadelphia nonprofit that works to stop punishing women and girls who are survivors of gender violence. It gives legal help, pushes for policy change, trains court and police staff, and takes on volunteers and interns.
records.what_you_do: Volunteers bring skills such as legal help, research, counseling, teaching, photography and fundraising. Interns do research and writing, outreach, advocacy campaigns, and parole and commutation paperwork.

first_step.how: Email info@phillyjusticeproject.org to talk about which volunteer role fits your skills, interests and availability.
first_step.basis: The group invites anyone to start with an email about volunteering. The site names no application steps, open roles or training, and its internships are unpaid and aimed at students.
first_step.what_to_expect: Your first step is an email conversation about your skills, your interests and how much time you can give. The site does not describe shifts, training or a time commitment, so ask about those in your first email. Internships are unpaid and hybrid, with in-person meetings, court hearings and sometimes visits to prison and jail facilities.
first_visit_tips: Write a short email about your skills and the hours you can give.
Ask about time commitment, training and whether a role is remote or in person, since the site does not say.
For an internship, check eligibility: the page lists law students, graduate students in the social sciences, and advanced undergraduates.
For an internship, expect travel to court hearings and to prison and jail facilities.

records.notes: The tier 1 volunteers link (/volunteers) is replaced by /volunteers-interns/. The newest dated item with a year is an April 25, 2025 court event. No 2026 events or news were found on the site. Internships are unpaid. An undergraduate chapter ran from 2020 to 2025, and the page invites inquiries about starting a new local chapter.

records.name: Philadelphia Legacies
records.summary: Gives commissioned portraits and leadership awards to Philadelphians who serve their communities. It also runs networking dinners and historic tours, and donations help young people and emerging leaders attend at low or no cost.
records.what_you_do: Buy a ticket to the yearly awards, a dinner or a tour, or donate to help others attend.

schedule.text: The main awards gala is held once a year. Networking dinners and historic tours are posted on the site with their own dates.

cost.text: Tickets are sold for the awards gala, dinners and tours. Prices were not shown on the pages read, which mention a ticket donation amount without a figure.

first_step.how: Buy a ticket to the next awards gala, a dinner or a tour on the Buy Tickets page, or use the Get Involved link on the contact page to ask about events.
first_step.basis: Events are open to the public but sold as tickets, prices are not shown on the pages read, and the Get Involved path leads mostly to sponsors and donors.
first_step.what_to_expect: The awards gala is an evening event at the Restaurant School at Walnut Hill College, where community leaders receive commissioned portraits and awards. Single tickets and tables are sold, and the ticket page offers tables of ten. Historic tours cover sites in Germantown, Center City and South Philadelphia, and Wynnefield and West Philadelphia, but the tour pages give no dates, meeting places or prices.
first_visit_tips: Check the Buy Tickets page for current prices before you plan.
Plan for a long evening, since the gala runs from late afternoon into the night.
Ask through the contact page about tour dates and meeting places, since they are not posted.
Decide between a single ticket and a table, since both are sold.

records.notes: The awards gala dated 10/03/2026 on the Buy Tickets page is the basis for last_sign_of_life. The tour pages list stops in three areas but no dates, prices or meeting places. The ticket page offers a 50 percent discount code, which was left out as a promotion. Named partners (not checked, see leads_only): CultureWorks Greater Philadelphia as fiscal sponsor. Sponsors named on the site include the Philadelphia Phillies, Independence Blue Cross Foundation, Seligsohn Foundation and Temple University.

records.name: Philadelphia Martin Luther King Jr. Association for Nonviolence
records.summary: A Philadelphia group that teaches nonviolence and runs family help, including a monthly food distribution and a holiday toy drive for children.
records.what_you_do: Join a nonviolence workshop or a College for Teens program for high school students, ask about the monthly food distribution (delivery is also available), or apply for the holiday toy drive if your family qualifies.

schedule.text: Food distribution happens monthly, but the day and time are not published. The holiday toy drive runs once a year around the winter holidays. Workshop and class dates are not published.

cost.text: College for Teens costs students nothing, according to the page. The page lists no fees for the food distribution or the toy drive.

first_step.how: Call 215-751-9300 or use the contact form on philadelphiamlk.org to ask about the next College for Teens session or the monthly food distribution. For the toy drive, follow the application steps on the toy page.
first_step.basis: Workshops and food help are listed, but the site gives no workshop dates, food distribution times or sign-up steps. College for Teens and the toy drive use applications and eligibility rules.
first_step.what_to_expect: College for Teens is aimed at low-income students from minority communities, starting around age 12 in grade 7, and it runs through college. Its parts include after-school tutoring, a summer residency on a college campus, and year-round mentoring and career exposure, at no cost to students. The food distribution and toy drive are for families who qualify, and the toy drive needs an online application with proof that the children live with you and proof of income.
first_visit_tips: The office is on the 7th floor at 3001 Walnut Street, according to the site footer.
For the toy drive, gather proof that the children live with you and proof of your income before you apply.
Ask about College for Teens session dates by phone or the contact form, since the site does not list them.
Watch for the toy drive email, which the page says arrives in early December, and check your spam folder.

records.notes: The site footer and program pages give 3001 Walnut Street, 7th Floor, Philadelphia, PA 19111, but this record keeps the 19104 zip from our earlier data. Please verify the zip. The toy drive page asks families not to call the office or Toys for Tots and gives a Gmail address for help. That is unusual, so the Gmail address is not in this record and this record does not send families there. The early December notice on the toy page, which says applications are being accepted now, is the basis for last_sign_of_life. The workshop pages carry no details.

records.name: Philadelphia Office of Immigrant Affairs
records.summary: The City of Philadelphia office that creates programs for immigrant residents and helps them connect to city services and civic life. Each September it runs Welcoming Week, a set of public events.
records.what_you_do: Attend a Welcoming Week event in September, come to the yearly Welcoming Awards, or sign up for the office newsletter.

schedule.text: Welcoming Week is a yearly series of community events each September across the city, and some events need you to register. The office also holds an annual Welcoming Awards ceremony.

first_step.how: Sign up for the office newsletter, then register for a Welcoming Week event that interests you (some events need registration).
first_step.basis: Events are open to the public, several have registration links, and the office has a newsletter sign up. The site names no volunteer sign up.
first_step.what_to_expect: Welcoming Week events are public sessions across the city, such as exhibits, civic resource workshops, arts festivals and a wellness workshop. They are aimed at immigrants and the wider community, and the office's pages do not give event prices. Check each listing for the time, place and whether you need to register.
first_visit_tips: Pick an event from the Welcoming Week list and check whether it asks you to register.
Sign up for the newsletter to hear about new events as they are posted.
Call (215) 686-0876 or email OIA@phila.gov if you have questions about city services.

records.notes: The city's Welcoming Week page gives the 2026 edition as September 10 to 25, 2026, with the Welcoming Awards on October 1, 2026. The 2025 edition ran September 12 to 21, 2025. The 2020 page from tier 1 is old and is not the basis for the yearly claim. The office page lists an African Immigrant Heritage event dated September 1, 2027, which is not part of the 2026 Welcoming Week, so it was not used. The office page names two Mayor's commissions it supports; they are in leads_only, not checked.

records.name: Philly Free School
records.summary: A school where students learn at their own pace and help govern it through a direct democracy, with tuition and open houses for families.
records.what_you_do: Families can fill out the interest form, come to an Open House, or book a virtual Q and A to learn about admissions. The school also rents its space and takes gifts to its annual appeal.

schedule.text: School hours are 8:30 am to 4 pm, Monday through Friday, and the school enrolls students all year. Extended care before or after school may be offered for an extra fee.

cost.text: Tuition is a sliding scale set through a third party called FACTS. For 2025 to 2026 the range was $1,800 to $17,800 a year, and a $50 application fee applies. The school says scholarships and programs help families for whom the lower end is still hard to pay.

access.notes: The school says outside organizations that offer special needs support can deliver those services at the school.

first_step.how: Fill out the interest form on phillyfreeschool.org, then come to an Open House (children are welcome) or book a virtual Q and A.
first_step.basis: The site lays out the steps for new families: an interest form, an Open House, an application with a $50 fee, a conversation with the family, and a trial week at the school.
first_step.what_to_expect: The first conversation is an informal talk with the parents or guardians and the prospective student, not a typical school interview. It is followed by a full trial week at the school so both sides can check the fit. The school day runs 8:30 am to 4 pm, Monday to Friday, and tuition is set on a sliding scale by family finances.
first_visit_tips: Bring your child to the Open House, since children are welcome there.
If you cannot visit in person, ask about a virtual Q and A session.
Apply for tuition help through FACTS, since the scale depends on family finances.
Plan transport for the 8:30 am to 4 pm school day, and ask about extended care if you need it.

records.notes: Tuition figures come from the tuition page for 2025 to 2026. The FAQ shows 2024 to 2025 figures of $1,800 to $17,000, so the site is not consistently current. No age or grade range appears on the pages read. The events page lists no open houses, so Open House dates are not published. The Open House RSVP form is linked on the home page.

records.name: Philadelphia Science Fiction Society
records.summary: A society for science fiction and fantasy fans in Philadelphia. It holds free meetings most months with guest speakers, author talks and fan panels.
records.what_you_do: Come to meetings, which are all free and open to the public, to hear guest speakers and authors and join fan panels. The November meeting is held in person at PHILCON.

schedule.text: Most months on a Friday evening, usually at 8 pm, alternating between Zoom and in-person meetings. The annual Hugo review panel meets at 7:30 pm.

cost.text: Meetings are free and open to the public. Membership is optional, with yearly dues of $48 for one person or $84 for a couple.

first_step.how: Come to a Friday meeting, on Zoom or in person at St. Mary's at Penn or the Rotunda, then email info@psfs.org to get on the announcement list.
first_step.basis: Meetings are free and open to anyone, membership is not needed to attend, and the page gives an email contact. It does not describe a welcome for newcomers.
first_step.what_to_expect: Meetings usually feature a guest speaker, such as a physicist or an author, and some are in person while others are on Zoom. Attending is free and you do not need to be a member. If you want to join later, the page says you become eligible for membership after three in-person meetings, which can be spread over months or years.
first_visit_tips: For the three in-person meetings that count toward membership, pick St. Mary's at Penn or the Rotunda.
Check the meetings page before you go, since some meetings are virtual.
At St. Mary's at Penn, the meeting room is in the parish building behind the sanctuary.
Email info@psfs.org if you want the announcement list or have questions.

records.notes: The meetings page names 2026 for the September and December meetings in its body text, which is the basis for last_sign_of_life. The October 9 and November 20 entries have no year written, so they were not used as dated evidence. The site gives 3916 Locust Walk in one place and 3916 Locust Street in another. This record keeps Locust Walk from our earlier data, so please verify it.
